overview: This atlas record starts in 1960 but draws Vietnam as one country during a period of separate northern and southern governments. The South Vietnamese state fell in 1975; formal reunification as the Socialist Republic followed in 1976. The imported modern name therefore cannot describe every government within the map’s full time span.

periods.title: A divided country at war
periods.summary: Northern and southern governments, Vietnamese revolutionary forces and foreign powers fought over the country’s future.

periods.title: Military victory and transition
periods.summary: The southern state ended in 1975; formal reunification into the Socialist Republic occurred the following year.

periods.title: Reconstruction and further conflict
periods.summary: Postwar restructuring, displacement and wars involving Cambodia and China marked a difficult decade.

periods.title: Doi Moi and economic transformation
periods.summary: Reforms begun in 1986 expanded market activity and connections to the world economy, helping reduce poverty.

periods.title: Institutions and changing everyday life
periods.summary: The 2013 Constitution restated the Communist Party’s leading role and recognized Vietnamese as the national language.

items.text: The 1960 outline hides a crucial division. After the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, the Geneva settlement provided for a temporary military separation near the seventeenth parallel. Northern and southern governments controlled separate parts of the country. This broad atlas polygon is not a map of either side’s actual control.

During the war, northern regular forces and southern communist forces fought the Republic of Vietnam and its allies, including the United States. China and the Soviet Union supported the communist side. US forces withdrew in 1973; the South Vietnamese army surrendered when Saigon fell on 30 April 1975.

On 2 July 1976, the formally reunited country took the name Socialist Republic of Vietnam. Military victory and the legal creation of the united state were related events, but they were not the same date. Earlier colonial Annam and Cochinchina, and medieval Vietnamese kingdoms, require their own historical accounts.

Reunification brought coercive political and economic restructuring as well as rebuilding. The authorities sought to transform southern commerce and farming, while many families feared persecution or losing property. People who had lived through war did not automatically share the same experience of the peace that followed.

Fighting also continued beyond Vietnam’s borders. Vietnamese forces invaded Cambodia in December 1978 and removed the Khmer Rouge government, followed by a prolonged occupation. China attacked northern Vietnam in 1979. The end of the earlier war had not brought an immediate end to regional conflict.

Many Vietnamese left by sea in the postwar years, facing crowded boats and serious danger. In May 1979, UNHCR and Vietnam agreed on an orderly-departure programme intended as a safer alternative. These movements scattered families across countries, while humanitarian programmes also supported schools, wells and clinics inside Vietnam.

The 2013 Constitution identifies the Communist Party as the leading force in state and society. It also describes representative institutions and rights for different ethnic communities. A constitutional text tells us how a state defines its authority and commitments; it does not by itself establish how every person experiences those commitments.

The reforms called Doi Moi began in 1986 and helped turn a very poor economy into a middle-income one. Market activity, international exchange and expanded infrastructure changed opportunities for work and education. The World Bank attributes the transformation to both domestic reforms and favourable global conditions, rather than to a single invention or leader.

A World Bank assessment published in 2022 found that falling poverty had not made every household secure. Ethnic and regional differences remained, and families above the poverty line could still be vulnerable to costly shocks. A country can grow richer while a lost job or illness remains a serious household problem.

The war left explosives in fields and villages long after the fighting ended. In a 2019 UNDP account, specialists cleared contaminated land while children in Binh Dinh learned through drawings and quizzes. Ten-year-old Ngoc drew soldiers and residents dealing with the remnants: recovery included making ordinary places safer for another generation.

sections.title: Family gatherings, food and skilled hands

items.text: For many families, Tet is a time to return home, remember ancestors and visit relatives. Children may receive envelopes of lucky money from elders. An official tourism account also describes classmates visiting teachers with fruit and flowers. The celebration reaches beyond the dining table into networks of family, neighbours and school.

Tet foods include square banh chung and cylindrical banh tet, made with sticky rice and fillings such as mung beans and pork. They need hours of cooking. Southern tables may also feature pork and duck eggs simmered with coconut juice and fish sauce, with candied fruit ready for visitors.

Water puppets perform on a stage that is also a pool. The puppeteers stand in water and move lacquered, buoyant wooden figures using bamboo sticks and strings. Scenes of village life, festivals and comic characters can unfold across the surface. In this theatre, the backstage job is unusually wet.

Dong Ho printmakers in Bac Ninh carve pictures into wooden blocks and prepare natural pigments by hand. UNESCO’s 2025 account describes special paper coated with scallop powder and colours printed in sequence, with black outlines added last. A picture can require careful planning long before the final outline appears.

Dong Ho prints can show daily life, history, landscapes or subjects of worship. The wooden blocks themselves become family heirlooms, passed to the next generation along with skills learned from experienced makers. UNESCO placed the craft on its urgent-safeguarding list in 2025, when only a small number of families continued it.

Tau, a Mong teacher from Lao Cai, remembered struggling at school because he did not understand Vietnamese. In 2008 he joined a bilingual education pilot. Young pupils could begin learning through Mong while gradually developing Vietnamese, making the classroom a place where their first language was useful rather than an obstacle.

One of Tau’s former pupils, De, described showing written Mong words to his mother: she could not read them, but knew their meanings. The programme connected new literacy with family knowledge. It also helped children learn subjects such as mathematics without first having to solve a language puzzle in every sentence.

At Pu Nhi Primary School in Dien Bien, teachers had once fetched water early each morning. A UNICEF report published in March 2023 describes improvements supported from 2019: filtration equipment, ceramic filters, handwashing stations and new latrines. Water infrastructure was as much part of school life as the classroom itself.

Ten-year-old Nisa showed UNICEF the old well and used the new handwashing facilities during recess. Her school also had gardens and space for football. The report records children’s pleasure in being able to wash and use school toilets, small comforts that become very noticeable when they have been missing.

At Long Phu C Primary School in Soc Trang, a UNICEF project introduced a toilet system designed to use solar energy to treat wastewater for reuse in flushing. The story describes the equipment arriving for installation, rather than a completed national rollout. The clever part is giving toilet water another useful job.

In October 2024, WHO validated Vietnam’s elimination of trachoma as a public-health problem after decades of work. The campaign combined surgery and antibiotics with facial cleanliness and better surroundings, including water and sanitation. This was a major prevention achievement, while continued monitoring remained necessary; elimination did not mean the infection had vanished from the planet.

A WHO report in 2025 recorded no malaria deaths in Vietnam during 2024, while noting that transmission remained in some areas. Health workers in remote communities and a network of provincial, district and commune services contributed to the progress. The report described a push toward elimination, not an announcement that malaria was already gone.

Hanoi-born Ngo Bao Chau won a Fields Medal in 2010 for proving the Fundamental Lemma, a difficult mathematical result connecting several areas of advanced mathematics. He used geometric methods to resolve a longstanding problem. His education and career linked Vietnam, France and the United States: discovery often grows through international communities of researchers.

Exploration of Son Doong in 2009 revealed an extraordinary cave passage beneath the Phong Nha-Ke Bang landscape. UNESCO’s 2015 assessment emphasized its enormous diameter and continuous length, alongside the region’s underground rivers and many cave forms. Modern survey work made the scale clearer; it did not create the cave or imply that local people had never known its entrance.

Article 5.3 of the government’s online 2013 Constitution reads: Ngôn ngữ quốc gia là tiếng Việt. Translation: “The national language is Vietnamese.” The accents are part of the original Latin-based Vietnamese writing, not decoration. The same article recognizes communities’ rights to use their own languages and scripts.

ending.text: Vietnam continues as a country. Its modern economic transformation has brought major gains, while households still face uneven opportunities. The end of a war or a change in economic policy does not mean the end of a society.
